File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 297, Issue: Python version compatibility: `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (called in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` and relied on via the
`except queue.ShutDown` handling in `OrderedQueueWorker.run`) only exists in Python 3.13+.
On earlier supported Python versions this raises AttributeError, so shutdown will fail
(caught and logged per-queue, but workers will never exit via this path and `join(timeout=5.0)`
will time out, leaving daemon threads spinning on `work_queue.get()` forever). Verify the
minimum Python version for this service, or implement shutdown with sentinel values /
`queue.Queue.unfinished_tasks` signaling instead.

File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 133, Issue: Data loss on processing error: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in a `finally` block even when
`result_processor` raised, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`'s exception handler
also marks failed messages as complete. This means a message whose processing failed is
treated as done and its offset becomes committable — the message is permanently lost
(at-most-once delivery). This directly contradicts the class docstring "Only commits offsets
after successful processing". If at-most-once is intentional, the docstring should say so;
otherwise failed items should leave the offset outstanding so the partition is not committed
past them.

File: src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py, Line: 337, Issue: Possible Bug: `terminate()` sets `shutdown_event` but never joins `commit_thread`, unlike `close()`.
Since arroyo's `terminate()` is used for abrupt shutdown this may be acceptable, but the
commit thread can still be mid-`commit_function` when the process tears down, committing
offsets concurrently with shutdown. Also note `join()` delegates to `close()`, which
triggers a full graceful shutdown — confirm this matches the arroyo `ProcessingStrategy`
contract expected by the surrounding pipeline (join is normally a wait-only operation).

File: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py, Line: 246, Issue: Flaky test assertion: In `test_stats_reporting`, immediately after submitting 10 items the test asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. Since the pool's worker threads run concurrently with the test thread, all items may already have been processed (and the queue drained) before `get_stats()` is called, making this assertion intermittently fail. The subsequent `total_items == 0` assertion after the completion event is safe, but the first one depends on scheduling. Consider asserting on cumulative processed counts or removing the racy check.

File: tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py, Line: 96, Issue: Flaky distribution assertion: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash to exactly all 3 queue indices (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). Using fixed keys with a known mapping, or asserting a weaker property (e.g., consistency rather than full coverage), would be more robust.

File: tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py, Line: 1689, Issue: Resource leak on failure: In all the new `test_thread_queue_parallel_*` tests, `factory.shutdown()` is called after the assertions rather than in a `try/finally`. Wrap the test body in `try/finally` with `factory.shutdown()` in the `finally` block.

findings: File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go, Line: 100, Issue: Race condition: The limit enforcement in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is a non-atomic check-then-act: it counts devices, and if under the limit, proceeds to insert. Two concurrent requests can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, exceeding the limit. Under concurrent anonymous traffic (the exact scenario a device limit targets), the limit can be silently exceeded. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a transaction with a locking read, or a conditional insert based on the count).

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go, Line: 73, Issue: Inconsistent time windows: The limit check in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` counts devices using `time.Now()` as the window reference, while `updateDevice` uses `device.UpdatedAt` as the reference for the 30-day window. If the incoming device's `UpdatedAt` differs from the server's current time (e.g., clock skew, or a client-supplied/backfilled timestamp), the two code paths evaluate different device sets: a device may be counted toward the limit yet not be updatable by `updateDevice` (its `updated_at` falls outside the window relative to `device.UpdatedAt`), causing `ErrDeviceLimitReached` even though the device exists. Using a consistent reference time (e.g., `time.Now()` in both) would avoid this.

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go, Line: 84, Issue: Misleading error semantics: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `rowsAffected == 0`, but zero rows affected can also mean the device simply does not exist (or its `updated_at` is outside the window), not that the limit was reached. Callers distinguishing these cases (e.g., to log or return different errors to the user) will get a wrong signal. If conflating them is intentional, a comment or a distinct error/wrapping would make the contract clear.

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go, Line: 44, Issue: Synchronous tagging on auth path: TagDevice was previously run in a background goroutine with a detached context and a 2-minute timeout, so failures or slowness never affected authentication. It is now called synchronously with the request context on every anonymous authentication. If the backing store (anonstore) is slow or unavailable, every anonymous request will block or fail on tagging, adding latency to the hot auth path. Consider whether the device-limit check needs to be inline, or whether tagging can remain async with only the limit check synchronous.

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go, Line: 44, Issue: Request context for tagging: TagDevice now receives the request-scoped ctx instead of a detached context with its own timeout. If the client disconnects or the request is cancelled mid-authentication, tagging is aborted and the device may never be recorded, which could undercount devices and interact incorrectly with the new device-limit enforcement. The previous code deliberately used context.Background() with a timeout for this reason.

File: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go, Line: 144, Issue: Behavior change: `TagDevice` now returns the error from `tagDeviceUI` instead of only logging it and returning nil. This changes the contract for all callers: a UI-tagging failure (previously treated as non-fatal) now propagates as an error. If any caller treats a returned error as a request failure (e.g., aborts login or middleware processing), previously-tolerated transient store errors will now surface to users. findings: File: packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts, Line: 9, Issue: Breaking signature change: `getCalendar` is converted from a synchronous function to an async one (now returns a Promise). Every existing caller that used the returned `Calendar | null` synchronously will now receive a Promise instead, silently breaking type checks and runtime behavior (e.g., `getCalendar(credential).lib` would be undefined). All call sites must be updated to `await` the result; no test coverage is added for this change.

File: packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts, Line: 14, Issue: Await semantics assumption: `await appStore[...]` assumes each appStore entry is either a Promise (from a top-level dynamic `import()`) or a plain value. If the async refactor changed appStore entries to be lazy factory functions (e.g., `() => import(...)`), awaiting the function itself would not load the module and `calendarApp.lib` would be undefined, causing every calendar type to log "not implemented" and return null. Verify the shape of the appStore entries matches what is awaited here.

File: packages/app-store/index.ts, Line: 3, Issue: Type change to Promises: Each entry of `appStore` changed from a module namespace object to a `Promise<module>` (dynamic `import()`). Any consumer that accesses properties synchronously (e.g., `appStore.googlecalendar.someExport`) will now get `undefined` at runtime and TypeScript type errors, unless every call site in the PR was updated to `await` the promise. If any consumer of `appStore` was not updated, this breaks app loading at runtime. Verify all usages were migrated to the async form.

File: packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts, Line: 125, Issue: Unawaited async callback: Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` means the returned promises are not awaited by `forEach`, so the `try` block completes before any of the calendar deletions finish. Any rejection from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` (or from `getCalendar`) becomes an unhandled promise rejection and will never be caught by the surrounding `try`/`catch`, so failures to delete calendar events are silently lost. Use `for...of` with `await` (or `Promise.all` over mapped promises) so errors propagate to the existing error handling.

File: packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts, Line: 125, Issue: Unhandled async in forEach: The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` is now `async`, but `forEach` ignores the returned promise. As a result: (1) the enclosing `try` block cannot catch any rejection from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting`, so a failed calendar deletion is silently swallowed instead of being handled by the surrounding error handling; (2) the caller of `Reschedule` cannot know when (or whether) the deletions complete. A concrete trigger: if `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` rejects for one booking ref, the error never reaches the `try`/`catch` around the loop. Consider `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all` over mapped promises.

File: packages/core/CalendarManager.ts, Line: 28, Issue: Unawaited promise: In `getCalendarCredentials`, `getCalendar(credential)` is now asynchronous (this PR converts it to return a Promise), but the result is stored unawaited in the `calendar` field of each entry. While `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`, any other consumer of the array returned by `getCalendarCredentials` that reads `calendar` directly (e.g., checks `if (!calendar)` or calls `calendar.someMethod()`) will now operate on a Promise object instead of a calendar instance, silently changing behavior. If `getCalendarCredentials` is exported and used elsewhere, those call sites need the same treatment.

This is on the hot path of `getBusyVideoTimes`, which previously fanned out availability checks concurrently. Consider `Promise.all` over the lookups (or at least be aware of the added latency when a booking has several video credentials). Low severity, but a real regression in latency introduced by this change.
